course.title: Social Entrepreneurship
course.description: Social entrepreneurship uses the tools of business to tackle social and environmental problems, sitting deliberately between ordinary commerce and traditional charity. This course explains how such ventures define their mission, pick a legal form, build a revenue model, raise money, measure the good they create, and grow their impact without losing their way. Structure and framing are adapted from the article on Social entrepreneurship in Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Social entrepreneurship is best described as using...
options: business tools mainly to maximize profit for owners
business tools primarily to solve a social or environmental problem
donations only, exactly like a traditional charity
government budgets to run public services
questions.explanation: A social entrepreneur's primary purpose is solving a social or environmental problem; finance is a means to sustain that work.

questions.prompt: Compared with a traditional charity, a social enterprise usually...
options: earns at least part of its income by selling goods or services
is forbidden from helping poor people
questions.explanation: The defining move is earning trading income, so the mission does not depend only on outside gifts.

questions.prompt: The triple bottom line refers to...
questions.explanation: People, planet, and profit - that is, social, environmental, and financial value together.

questions.prompt: In a theory of change, counting the number of workshops a venture ran is a measure of...
questions.explanation: A count of activity is an output; it is not yet a changed life, which would be an outcome.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit organization is defined by the rule that it...
questions.explanation: A nonprofit may trade and pay staff, but any surplus must be reinvested in the mission, not paid out to owners.

questions.prompt: A Certified B Corporation is...
options: a legal form set by statute
a private certification awarded after an audit
questions.explanation: A B Corp is a certification from the nonprofit B Lab, distinct from the benefit corporation legal form.

questions.prompt: In the cross-subsidy model, the paying customer and the person who benefits are...
questions.explanation: Paying customers fund goods or services for others who cannot pay, so payer and beneficiary differ.

questions.prompt: Muhammad Yunus is best known for founding...
options: the Grameen Bank and microfinance for the poor
questions.explanation: Yunus and the Grameen Bank shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize for pioneering microloans to the very poor.

lessons.title: What social entrepreneurship is
lessons.grammar_note: A social enterprise is defined by its primary purpose, not by a single good deed - an occasional donation does not make an ordinary company a social enterprise.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define social entrepreneurship in your own words and place it between two familiar neighbors: the ordinary profit-seeking business and the traditional donation-funded charity. By the end you will be able to say what a social entrepreneur is actually trying to maximize, why that single goal shapes every later decision about money and form, and how to spot the difference when you read about a real venture. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is the one feature that most clearly separates a social enterprise from a company whose only aim is owner return? Hold your answer in mind - we will sharpen it as we go. You will also learn why the label is contested, since people use the same two words for a nonprofit running a thrift shop, a for-profit selling cheap eyeglasses in poor regions, and a global fund that backs both, and knowing the core test lets you cut through the marketing.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A social entrepreneur builds an organization whose primary purpose is to solve a social or environmental problem, and treats financial sustainability as a means to that end rather than the end itself. A traditional business exists to create private value for its owners; profit is the goal, and social benefit, if any, is a side effect. A traditional charity exists to create social value, but it usually funds itself through donations and grants rather than selling a product, so it depends on the continued goodwill of outside givers. Social entrepreneurship sits deliberately in the middle: it pursues a social mission, like a charity, but tries to earn at least part of its own income through trade, like a business. The promise of that middle position is durability, because a venture that pays its own way need not stop helping people the moment a grant runs out. The cost is tension, since mission and money can pull in opposite directions, and much of this course is about managing that pull honestly rather than pretending it is absent.

sections.heading: Key figures & examples
sections.text: Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh are the textbook example. Yunus lent tiny sums to very poor villagers, mostly women, who had no collateral and were ignored by ordinary banks. The loans let borrowers start small enterprises, the bank charged interest and was repaid, and the model spread worldwide; Yunus and Grameen shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize. Compare three organizations to feel the spectrum. A corner bakery sells bread to make money for its owner, a pure business. A food bank gives away donated meals and runs on grants, a pure charity. A bakery that trains and employs people leaving prison, sells its bread at market price, and reinvests the surplus in training is a social enterprise, because the trading and the mission are built into the same machine. Other widely cited names include Ashoka, which funds individual social entrepreneurs around the world. Reading about any of these, ask the same question: what is this organization trying to maximize, and where does its money come from?

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what does a social entrepreneur treat as the end, and what as the means? 2) Name one way a social enterprise differs from a pure charity. 3) Why can earned income make a mission more durable than donations alone? 4) Is every profitable company a social enterprise? 5) Classify a shop that sells coffee to fund scholarships and reinvests all surplus. Answers: 1) Social impact is the end; financial sustainability, including profit, is the means. 2) It earns at least part of its income by selling a product or service, instead of relying only on donations and grants. 3) Earned income does not vanish when a single grant ends, so the work can continue without waiting for the next gift. 4) No - a company counts as a social enterprise only when solving a social or environmental problem is its primary purpose, not a side effect. 5) A social enterprise: it trades like a business but exists to fund and deliver a social mission.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming that any business which does some good, such as a one-off donation or a recycling bin, is a social enterprise. The test is the primary purpose, not an occasional gesture. Mistake: assuming a social enterprise must be a nonprofit. The legal form is a separate choice, covered later; what matters here is the mission-first intent. Mistake: treating charity as a lesser or failed version of social entrepreneurship. A charity serving people who can never pay is often exactly the right tool, and forcing a revenue model onto it can do real harm. Exit: (a) What does a social entrepreneur aim to maximize? (b) Name the two neighbors between which social entrepreneurship sits. Answers: social or environmental impact, with finance as a means to sustain it; the traditional profit-seeking business on one side and the traditional donation-funded charity on the other.

lessons.title: The double bottom line, blended value, and theory of change
lessons.grammar_note: Outputs count what you did; outcomes count what changed for people - keep the two words apart, because swapping them is the most common way ventures overstate their results.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a social venture measures beyond money, and lay out the causal story that connects what it does to the change it hopes to cause. You will be able to define the double and triple bottom line, say what blended value means, and sketch a simple theory of change using the chain of inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and impact. Warm-up: a job-training charity reports that it ran forty workshops last year. Is that a measure of effort or a measure of change in people's lives? Keep that distinction close, because confusing the two is the most common error in this whole field. By the end you should be able to take any venture's cheerful annual report and ask, politely but firmly, where is the evidence that the world is actually different because you existed? You will also see why sensible people disagree about how far to push measurement before it becomes a costly distraction from the work itself.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A conventional business keeps one bottom line: profit. The double bottom line adds a second, social value, and the triple bottom line adds a third, environmental value, often summarized as people, planet, and profit. Blended value is the related idea that value is not really separate at all - that every organization creates an inseparable mix of financial, social, and environmental value, and that splitting them into rival columns is artificial. A theory of change is the explicit, written-down logic that links a venture's work to its intended effect. The standard chain runs: inputs, such as money, staff, and time, fuel activities, the things you do like running workshops, which produce outputs, countable results like trainees served, which lead to outcomes, real changes in people such as getting and keeping a job, which add up to impact, the lasting difference in the wider world. The discipline is to be honest about where the chain is proven and where it is only hoped for. Stating the theory out loud makes those hopeful links visible, so they can be tested rather than quietly assumed.

sections.heading: Key figures & examples
sections.text: The phrase triple bottom line was popularized by John Elkington in the 1990s, who later said he wished people used it to rethink capitalism rather than merely to tidy up reporting. Jed Emerson is credited with developing the blended value idea. Take a concrete venture: a social enterprise that employs homeless people to clean streets. Inputs are wages and equipment; the activity is cleaning; the output is kilometers of street cleaned and the number of people employed; the outcome is formerly homeless workers gaining stable income and housing; the hoped-for impact is a measurable fall in long-term homelessness in the city. Notice that the first three links are easy to count and the last two are hard and slow to prove, which is exactly why ventures are tempted to report outputs and quietly imply outcomes. A triple-bottom-line view would also track the environmental side, such as waste diverted from landfill, so that a win on one line is not secretly bought with a hidden loss on another.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three parts of the triple bottom line. 2) In the chain of change, is the number of workshops run an output or an outcome? 3) What is the outcome that sits beyond that output? 4) What does blended value claim about the three kinds of value? 5) Why is it dishonest to report only outputs? 6) Give one input in a street-cleaning enterprise. Answers: 1) People, planet, and profit - that is, social, environmental, and financial value. 2) An output; it counts activity, not changed lives. 3) An outcome such as learners gaining and keeping better jobs. 4) That financial, social, and environmental value are inseparable parts of one whole, not rival columns. 5) Because outputs show effort, and letting readers assume effort equals impact hides that the hard links in the chain may be unproven. 6) Wages, equipment, or staff time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing outputs with outcomes - counting the forty workshops and calling it impact. Outputs measure what you did; outcomes measure what changed for people. Mistake: treating a theory of change as paperwork for funders, then filing it away. Its value is as a testable claim you keep checking against reality. Mistake: assuming more measurement is always better. Past a point, elaborate metrics can cost more than the programs they track and can crowd out plain judgment, so measure what you will actually use. This is why honest ventures write down the whole chain and mark which links are evidenced and which are still hopes. Exit: (a) Give the five-link chain from resources to lasting change, in order. (b) Which link is usually easy to count, and which is usually hard to prove? Answers: inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact; outputs are easy to count, while outcomes and impact are hard and slow to prove.

lessons.title: Legal forms: nonprofit, for-profit, hybrid, and the B Corp
lessons.grammar_note: A benefit corporation is a legal status set by statute; a Certified B Corporation is a private certificate from B Lab - they sound alike, but a company can hold either, both, or neither.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose, or at least reason clearly about, the legal wrapper a social venture should use, and explain the trade-offs of each. You will be able to tell a nonprofit from a for-profit, describe what a hybrid structure tries to achieve, and say what a benefit corporation is and how it differs from a Certified B Corporation - two things that sound alike and are constantly confused. Warm-up: if your venture needs to raise large amounts of investment and also wants a legal duty to pursue its mission, which single traditional form gives you both? The honest answer is neither cleanly, which is exactly why hybrids exist. Keep in mind throughout that the legal form is a tool chosen to fit the mission and the money, not a badge of virtue; a nonprofit is not automatically more ethical than a for-profit, and the structure should follow the strategy rather than the other way around.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A nonprofit, in many countries a charity, is barred from distributing profits to owners; any surplus must be reinvested in the mission. It can usually receive tax-deductible donations and grants but cannot sell equity to investors, which limits how fast it can raise growth capital. A for-profit can raise equity and move quickly, but its directors traditionally owe a duty to shareholders, so a purely mission-driven choice that lowers returns can expose them to pressure or legal risk. A hybrid structure tries to capture both sides, often by pairing a nonprofit with a for-profit subsidiary, so donations and investment can each flow to the part suited to them. The benefit corporation is a for-profit legal form, available in many places, that writes a public-benefit purpose into the company charter and legally permits, and sometimes requires, directors to weigh mission alongside profit. A Certified B Corporation is different: it is a private certification awarded by the nonprofit B Lab to companies that pass an audit of their social and environmental practices. One is a legal status set by statute; the other is a voluntary certificate.

sections.heading: Key figures & examples
sections.text: B Lab, founded in 2006, created and runs the B Corp certification, and well-known certified firms have included Patagonia and various consumer brands. The benefit corporation as a legal form first became available in Maryland in 2010 and has since spread to many jurisdictions. The two are independent: a company can be a legal benefit corporation without B Corp certification, can be a certified B Corp without being a statutory benefit corporation, can be both, or neither. A concrete case: a founder building a low-cost solar-lamp company that needs millions in investment will likely pick a for-profit, perhaps incorporated as a benefit corporation so the mission is protected when new investors arrive, and may also seek B Corp certification as a public signal. By contrast, a venture distributing free lamps to people who can never pay has no revenue to attract investors and fits a nonprofit. The lesson is that the same cause can call for opposite forms depending on who pays and how growth is funded.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What can a nonprofit not do with its surplus? 2) Why can a classic for-profit form create tension for a mission-driven founder? 3) What does a hybrid structure pair, and why? 4) Benefit corporation versus Certified B Corp - which is a legal status and which is a private certification? 5) Can a company be a benefit corporation without being a certified B Corp? Answers: 1) Distribute it to owners; surplus must be reinvested in the mission. 2) Directors owe a duty to shareholders, so sacrificing returns for mission can bring pressure or legal risk unless the form protects it. 3) A nonprofit with a for-profit arm, so grants and investment each flow to the part suited to receive them. 4) The benefit corporation is a legal status set by statute; the Certified B Corp is a private certification from B Lab. 5) Yes - the two are independent, so a firm can hold either, both, or neither.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using benefit corporation and B Corp as synonyms. One is a statutory legal form; the other is a certification from a private nonprofit, and a company may have one without the other. Mistake: believing a nonprofit cannot earn income. It can sell goods and services; it simply cannot pay profits out to owners. Mistake: picking a form to look virtuous rather than to fit how the venture will raise money and protect its mission. Exit: (a) Which form is barred from distributing profit to owners? (b) Name the structure that pairs two entities so it can take both donations and investment. (c) Is a benefit corporation a legal status or a certificate? Answers: the nonprofit; the hybrid, a nonprofit paired with a for-profit subsidiary; a legal status set by statute, as opposed to the B Corp certificate issued by B Lab.

lessons.title: Business models: cross-subsidy, employment, and fee-for-service
lessons.grammar_note: The question who pays, and is it the same person who benefits, sorts the main models - trace the cash before you trust the pitch.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the main ways a social enterprise actually earns money while advancing its mission, and match a model to a situation. You will be able to explain the cross-subsidy, employment or work-integration, and fee-for-service models, and recognize when the beneficiary and the paying customer are the same person and when they are not. Warm-up: a clinic wants to serve patients who cannot pay. Where could the money come from if not from those patients? Hold that question, because the answer defines the model. By the end you should be able to read a venture's one-line pitch and name the engine underneath it, which tells you far more about whether it will survive than any mission statement does. You will also see that most real ventures blend two or three of these models rather than running on just one, especially in their early years when trading income is still thin.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In the cross-subsidy model, the enterprise sells something to customers who can pay and uses the surplus to serve those who cannot; the paying and the benefiting groups are different people. A common version charges richer customers a higher price for the same good that poorer customers get cheaply or free. In the employment, or work-integration, model the social good is the job itself: the enterprise hires people who face barriers to work, such as the long-term unemployed, people with disabilities, or those leaving prison, and sells ordinary goods or services, so the paying customer funds the beneficiary's wage and training. In the fee-for-service model the beneficiary is the customer: the enterprise sells a mission-relevant product or service directly to the people it aims to help, often at a price they can afford, as with low-cost health screening or affordable schooling. Each model answers one question, who pays and are they the same person who benefits, and that single answer shapes marketing, pricing, and risk. Most durable ventures mix models, for instance combining fee-for-service income with grants during their early years.

sections.heading: Key figures & examples
sections.text: Cross-subsidy: Aravind Eye Care in India performs eye surgery, charging paying patients enough to cover free or subsidized operations for the poor, and stays self-sustaining at large scale. Employment: Greyston Bakery in New York practices open hiring, employing people regardless of background and selling its baked goods commercially, so buyers of the product fund the jobs. Fee-for-service: microfinance institutions such as the Grameen Bank sell a service, small loans, directly to poor borrowers who are also the beneficiaries. Notice how the question who pays sorts them. At Aravind the paying patient subsidizes the poor one. At Greyston the product buyer never meets the worker whose job they fund. At Grameen the borrower is both customer and beneficiary. A single venture can layer these: a job-training enterprise might sell catering, an employment model, while also charging corporate clients premium rates that subsidize placements, a cross-subsidy, and lean on grants until the trading income matures. Reading any social enterprise, trace the cash and you will find one of these engines, or a deliberate blend.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In the cross-subsidy model, are the paying customer and the beneficiary the same person? 2) What is the social good being delivered in the employment model? 3) In fee-for-service, who is the customer? 4) Classify a bakery that hires people leaving prison and sells bread commercially. 5) Classify a hospital that charges wealthy patients extra to fund free care for the poor. 6) Why do many ventures blend models? Answers: 1) No - different people; the payer funds service for someone else. 2) The job itself, including wages and training for people who face barriers to employment. 3) The beneficiary - the very person the venture aims to help buys the product or service. 4) The employment, or work-integration, model. 5) The cross-subsidy model. 6) To spread risk and bridge the early years, when trading income alone may not yet cover the mission, so grants and several revenue streams keep the venture alive.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a social enterprise must break even on day one. Many blend earned income with grants for years while the trading side matures, and that is a plan, not a failure. Mistake: confusing the employment model with simply having employees. The point is that hiring people who face barriers to work is the mission, not a byproduct. Mistake: pricing a fee-for-service product as if beneficiaries had rich-world budgets, which prices out the very people it is meant to serve. Exit: (a) Which model has the payer and the beneficiary be different people? (b) In which model is the beneficiary the paying customer? (c) In the employment model, what is the social product? Answers: the cross-subsidy model; the fee-for-service model; a job, with the wages and training that come with it, for people who would otherwise be shut out of work.

lessons.title: Measuring social impact and funding the work
lessons.grammar_note: The counterfactual question is always compared with what - credit a program only for change that would not have happened anyway.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how social ventures try to measure the good they do, and map the main ways they raise money. You will be able to name common impact measures and their limits, define the idea behind a social return on investment, and distinguish grants, philanthropy, impact investing, and earned revenue by what each one expects in return. Warm-up: two charities both say they lifted a thousand people out of poverty. One counted people who enrolled; the other compared results against a similar group who got no help. Which claim should you trust, and why? Keep that comparison in mind, because the hardest question in measurement is always what would have happened anyway. By the end you should be able to look at a funding pitch and ask what the money provider wants back, since a grant, an investment, and a gift each pull the venture in very different directions once the cash arrives.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Measuring social impact means estimating the change a venture caused, not just the activity it performed. The central difficulty is the counterfactual: what would have happened without the program. Strong evidence compares outcomes against a similar untreated group; weak evidence just counts participants. Social return on investment, or SROI, tries to express outcomes in money, estimating the social value created per unit spent, but the estimates rest on debatable assumptions and should be read with care. On the funding side, four sources dominate. Grants are sums, usually from foundations or governments, given for a defined purpose and expecting reporting but not repayment. Philanthropy, or donations, are gifts expecting only mission progress and perhaps recognition. Impact investing provides capital, as loans or equity, that expects both a financial return and measurable social impact, often accepting lower returns in exchange for the latter. Earned revenue is money the venture makes by selling goods or services, the most durable source because it carries no outside expectation beyond delivering the product. Most ventures build a stack, blending several sources as they grow.

sections.heading: Key figures & examples
sections.text: Impact investing as a named field grew after the term was coined around 2007, with networks and shared standards following; the Acumen fund, founded by Jacqueline Novogratz, is a well-known patient-capital investor backing enterprises that serve the poor. For measurement, the most rigorous tool is the randomized controlled trial, used by research groups to test whether programs such as microloans or free bed nets actually change outcomes; results have sometimes been humbling, showing smaller effects than advocates hoped. Consider a solar-lamp venture assembling a funding stack: a foundation grant funds early product design, a wealthy donor gives to a pilot as philanthropy, an impact fund lends to finance inventory expecting repayment with modest interest and evidence of lamps reaching poor households, and lamp sales cover day-to-day costs as earned revenue. Each source wants something different back - a report, a thank-you, a repaid loan plus impact data, or simply a working product - and the founder must keep all four satisfied without letting any one quietly distort the mission.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What makes a measured impact claim strong rather than weak? 2) What does SROI try to express, and what is its main weakness? 3) Which funding source expects the capital back plus measurable social impact? 4) Which source is the most durable, and why? 5) What does a grant expect in return? Answers: 1) Comparing outcomes against a similar group who did not get the help, so you estimate what would have happened anyway. 2) It expresses social outcomes in monetary terms, the value created per unit spent; its weakness is that it rests on debatable assumptions. 3) Impact investing - capital that wants a financial return and measurable impact. 4) Earned revenue, because it carries no outside expectation beyond delivering the product and does not end when a funder leaves. 5) Reporting on the defined purpose it funded, but not repayment.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: ignoring the counterfactual and crediting the program for changes that would have happened anyway. Always ask, compared with what? Mistake: treating an SROI figure as a hard fact rather than an estimate built on assumptions you can inspect and challenge. Mistake: confusing impact investing with philanthropy. An impact investor expects the money back, often with a return, while a philanthropist makes a gift; mixing them up leads to broken promises on both sides. Exit: (a) What is the counterfactual question in one short phrase? (b) Which expects more attached in return, philanthropy or impact investing? (c) Which single source is most durable? Answers: what would have happened without the program, that is, compared with what; impact investing expects far more, since it wants the capital back with measurable impact, while philanthropy is essentially a gift; earned revenue is the most durable source.

lessons.title: Scaling impact, famous examples, and hard trade-offs
lessons.grammar_note: Scaling impact is not the same as scaling an organization - sometimes the biggest impact comes from helping others copy you, not from growing yourself.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the main ways a social venture can grow its impact, recall the landmark examples that shaped the field, and reason honestly about the trade-offs that make this work hard. You will be able to distinguish scaling an organization from scaling the impact, describe routes such as direct growth, replication, and open sharing of a model, and name the central tension between mission and money that recurs at every stage. Warm-up: a successful job-training enterprise in one city wants ten times the impact. Must it become ten times bigger itself, or is there another way? Hold that, because the best answer is often no, do not grow the organization at all, but spread the idea instead. By the end you should be able to weigh a growth plan and a funding decision against the mission rather than against pride or headlines, and to spot when scaling would quietly betray the very people it claims to serve.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Scaling impact is not the same as scaling an organization. Impact can grow in three broad ways. Direct scaling means the organization itself gets bigger, serving more people in more places, which keeps control but is slow and capital-hungry. Replication means helping others copy the model, through franchising, affiliates, or training, trading some control for faster, cheaper spread. Open scaling means giving the model away by publishing the method so anyone can adopt it, which maximizes reach and sacrifices ownership entirely. Choosing among them depends on how much the model relies on a specific team and place. Underneath every choice sits one recurring trade-off: mission versus money. Growth needs capital, capital comes with expectations, and the pressure to show returns or hit targets can pull a venture toward serving the customers who pay best rather than the people who need help most, a drift called mission drift. Other hard trade-offs include measurement cost versus honesty, speed versus depth, and the risk that chasing scale turns a careful local success into a shallow national disappointment.

sections.heading: Key figures & examples
sections.text: The Grameen Bank and Muhammad Yunus remain the defining example, showing both the promise of microfinance and its limits, since later studies found its effects on poverty were real but more modest than the early enthusiasm claimed. Bill Drayton founded Ashoka in 1980 and helped popularize the very term social entrepreneur, backing individual changemakers rather than single organizations, a replication-minded bet on people. Aravind Eye Care scaled directly to become one of the largest eye-care providers in the world while staying financially self-sustaining through cross-subsidy. Fair-trade labeling scaled a model through open and shared standards rather than through one company. Each illustrates a different route: Grameen and Aravind grew largely by direct scaling, Ashoka by backing replicators, and fair trade by spreading a shared standard. Each also shows a trade-off up close: microfinance can overburden borrowers if pushed too hard, direct scaling demands huge capital, and shared standards can be diluted when too many actors adopt the label loosely. The field advances by learning from these honest limits, not by repeating the founding legends uncritically.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is scaling impact the same as making the organization bigger? 2) Name the three broad routes to greater impact. 3) Which route gives up the most control, and what does it gain? 4) What is mission drift, and what tends to cause it? 5) What did later research reveal about microfinance? Answers: 1) No - impact can grow without the organization growing, by spreading the model to others. 2) Direct scaling, growing the organization; replication, helping others copy it; and open scaling, giving the model away. 3) Open scaling gives up ownership entirely and gains the widest, cheapest reach. 4) Mission drift is sliding toward serving whoever pays best rather than whoever needs help most; it is driven by the expectations that come with growth capital and revenue targets. 5) That its benefits were real but more modest than the early claims, a healthy correction rather than a dismissal.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming bigger is always better, and that an organization must grow in order to grow its impact. Often the greater impact comes from helping others, even rivals, copy you. Mistake: taking on growth capital without noticing the expectations attached, then being surprised when those expectations bend the mission. Mistake: treating the founding legends as finished successes rather than live experiments with real limits, which stops you learning from what went wrong. Exit: (a) Name the three routes to scaling impact. (b) What is the core recurring trade-off in social entrepreneurship? (c) Give one example venture and the route it mainly used. Answers: direct scaling, replication, and open or shared scaling; the tension between mission and money, where capital and revenue pressure can cause mission drift; for example, Aravind Eye Care grew mainly by direct scaling, while Ashoka backed replicators and fair trade spread a shared standard.
